prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Building Interface 7 Building Interface Street-facing interfaces include street interface elements and street buildings, and are an important component of road space, affecting people’s spatial, visual, and activity experience of the road. Street buildings and structures can define road space; positive functions set on the ground floor can expand the activity space of the road and increase activity content; in addition, street-facing elements are also an important part of road landscape, determining the image of the road and even the city. By forming a continuous street wall, they provide road users with facilities such as shade and rest. Therefore, road design should also consider the corresponding street interface and coordinate various elements in an integrated manner. 7.1 Interface Elements 7.1.1 Commercial Outdoor Seating/Display Commercial outdoor seating/display is the outdoor extension of the commercial interface within the road, and is a form in which road activities are combined with commercial formats. According to the type of business, it is divided into retail outdoor display and catering outdoor seating/display. 1. Design Key Points A. In terms of layout, the effect of commercial outdoor seating/display is related to the type of business format, and differentiated outdoor seating/display strategies should be formulated according to the characteristics of the business format. a. Control-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with narrow sidewalks but high and complex pedestrian flow. A commercial outdoor seating/display area may be appropriately arranged to increase road activity space for residents. Figure 7.1-1 Schematic Diagram of Control-Oriented Layout b. Encouragement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with wide sidewalks, mostly open ground-floor interfaces along the street, and large pedestrian flow. Street-front businesses should be encouraged to set up commercial outdoor seating/display areas to provide a more vibrant and functionally diverse place for road activities. Figure 7.1-2 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Layout c. Enhancement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads where open interfaces exist along the street but pedestrian activity is relatively low. Commercial outdoor seating/display areas may be set up to increase road activity space, attract pedestrians to stop, and enhance road vitality. Figure 7.1-3 Schematic Diagram of Enhancement-Oriented Layout B. Business format guidance a. Encouragement-oriented: mainly leisure dining businesses of a certain grade. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business can not only increase road vitality, but also improve road quality. Figure 7.1-4 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Business Format Guidance b. Permissive: mainly fast-food dining businesses and various small- and medium-scale retail businesses. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business help enhance road vitality, but management should be strengthened and their arrangement standardized. Figure 7.1-5 Schematic Diagram of Permissive Business Format Guidance c. Prohibited: mainly various flavor-style dining businesses. Figure 2.1-3 Tidal Lane and Movable Barrier 2.1.3 Shared Lane 1. The design concept of shared roads emphasizes the integration of sidewalk and motor vehicle lane space. The use of shared-road space is pedestrian-oriented. In terms of functional space, it meets the different needs of different groups, including walking, cycling, and motor vehicles. In terms of planning concept, shared roads emphasize people-centered design, serving pedestrians and providing convenience for urban residents, making them more willing to gather in shared-road spaces. Figure 2.1-4 Street View of a Shared Road 2. The entire cross-section of a shared road is divided into a sidewalk and a shared carriageway. The sidewalk is exclusively for pedestrians and is integrated with the building frontage area. The shared carriageway is for all travelers; pedestrians, motor vehicles, and non-motorized vehicles may all travel on the shared carriageway. 3. A “time-limited pedestrian street” form may also be adopted, whereby motor vehicle access is prohibited during specified periods on part of the road, and a high-quality block combining commerce and culture is created in conjunction with the characteristics of the road section. 2.1.4 Median The median shall be enclosed with curb stones. Where anti-collision requirements need to be considered, anti-collision guardrails of the corresponding grade shall be used. When rainwater detention facilities need to be installed in the road median, the curb stone arrangement shall meet drainage requirements. 2.1.5 Bus-Only Lane 1. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 3 lanes or more (including 3 lanes), or the total one-way motor vehicle roadway width is not less than 11 m; where one-way passenger bus volume on the road section exceeds 6,000 persons/peak hour, or bus flow exceeds 150 vehicles/peak hour; and where the average section flow per lane exceeds 500 vehicles/peak hour. 2. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 4 lanes or more (including 4 lanes), and the one-way bus flow on the section exceeds 90 vehicles/peak hour. 3. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 2 lanes, the one-way passenger bus volume exceeds 6,000 persons/peak hour, and bus flow exceeds 150 vehicles/peak hour. 29 4. Bus-only lanes may be paved with colored asphalt. After paving, the lane color is conspicuous and forms a sharp contrast with the adjacent ordinary motor vehicle lane, preventing ordinary motor vehicles from mistakenly entering the lane. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

Spatial requirements: • Use road space efficiently and ensure sufficient slow-mobility space with shaded pedestrian areas. • Roads of this type should be designed with smaller turning radii. • Where conditions permit, motor-vehicle lanes may be compressed and a single-sided public-service/facility zone set up. • Actively create building setbacks, encourage buildings and sidewalks to be connected, maintain the same setback interface, and reduce the large variation between road-space and building-space. Facility requirements: • Provide convenient and safe pedestrian crossings; for life-service roads of higher grade, encourage elevated pedestrian crossings, curb extensions, and other traffic-calming facilities, and speed limits. • Encourage the use of green forms such as lawns, sparse tree stands, rows of trees, shrubs, and planting of trees and other vegetation to create a people-oriented, green environment. • Consider larger-canopy trees; for tall planting, the root space should be relatively small to ensure pedestrian passage space. • Use non-open interfaces on both sides as the main form; road greenery may be used to create transparent, screened, separated, and other visual-control effects. 9 Landscape-recreation roads Recommendations for upgrading and improving interface types General requirements: • Encourage the integration of urban landscape and recreational functions, balancing landscape and leisure activities with residents’ daily travel needs. • Increase the amount of green space along the line to avoid vegetation becoming an obstacle to activities. Spatial requirements: • Roads of this type should combine waterfront space and roadside green space, and use connected green spaces and widened building setbacks to create street-side open spaces. • In areas with abundant road space, pedestrian and bicycle lanes or dedicated motor-vehicle and non-motorized lanes may be set up, with public facilities arranged on one side. • Encourage the use of “sea-sponge city” technology, using side ditches, median strips, and roadside green belts, as well as smart rainwater-management facilities, to shape block-like or belt-like forms and to regulate and purify rainwater. Building Interface 7 Building Interface Street-facing interfaces include street interface elements and street buildings, and are an important component of road space, affecting people’s spatial, visual, and activity experience of the road. Street buildings and structures can define road space; positive functions set on the ground floor can expand the activity space of the road and increase activity content; in addition, street-facing elements are also an important part of road landscape, determining the image of the road and even the city. By forming a continuous street wall, they provide road users with facilities such as shade and rest. Therefore, road design should also consider the corresponding street interface and coordinate various elements in an integrated manner. 7.1 Interface Elements 7.1.1 Commercial Outdoor Seating/Display Commercial outdoor seating/display is the outdoor extension of the commercial interface within the road, and is a form in which road activities are combined with commercial formats. According to the type of business, it is divided into retail outdoor display and catering outdoor seating/display. 1. Design Key Points A. In terms of layout, the effect of commercial outdoor seating/display is related to the type of business format, and differentiated outdoor seating/display strategies should be formulated according to the characteristics of the business format. a. Control-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with narrow sidewalks but high and complex pedestrian flow. A commercial outdoor seating/display area may be appropriately arranged to increase road activity space for residents. Figure 7.1-1 Schematic Diagram of Control-Oriented Layout b. Encouragement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads with wide sidewalks, mostly open ground-floor interfaces along the street, and large pedestrian flow. Street-front businesses should be encouraged to set up commercial outdoor seating/display areas to provide a more vibrant and functionally diverse place for road activities. Figure 7.1-2 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Layout c. Enhancement-oriented layout strategy: applicable to roads where open interfaces exist along the street but pedestrian activity is relatively low. Commercial outdoor seating/display areas may be set up to increase road activity space, attract pedestrians to stop, and enhance road vitality. Figure 7.1-3 Schematic Diagram of Enhancement-Oriented Layout B. Business format guidance a. Encouragement-oriented: mainly leisure dining businesses of a certain grade. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business can not only increase road vitality, but also improve road quality. Figure 7.1-4 Schematic Diagram of Encouragement-Oriented Business Format Guidance b. Permissive: mainly fast-food dining businesses and various small- and medium-scale retail businesses. Outdoor seating/display areas of this type of business help enhance road vitality, but management should be strengthened and their arrangement standardized. Figure 7.1-5 Schematic Diagram of Permissive Business Format Guidance c. Prohibited: mainly various flavor-style dining businesses. Figure 2.1-3 Tidal Lane and Movable Barrier 2.1.3 Shared Lane 1. The design concept of shared roads emphasizes the integration of sidewalk and motor vehicle lane space. The use of shared-road space is pedestrian-oriented. In terms of functional space, it meets the different needs of different groups, including walking, cycling, and motor vehicles. In terms of planning concept, shared roads emphasize people-centered design, serving pedestrians and providing convenience for urban residents, making them more willing to gather in shared-road spaces. Figure 2.1-4 Street View of a Shared Road 2. The entire cross-section of a shared road is divided into a sidewalk and a shared carriageway. The sidewalk is exclusively for pedestrians and is integrated with the building frontage area. The shared carriageway is for all travelers; pedestrians, motor vehicles, and non-motorized vehicles may all travel on the shared carriageway. 3. A “time-limited pedestrian street” form may also be adopted, whereby motor vehicle access is prohibited during specified periods on part of the road, and a high-quality block combining commerce and culture is created in conjunction with the characteristics of the road section. 2.1.4 Median The median shall be enclosed with curb stones. Where anti-collision requirements need to be considered, anti-collision guardrails of the corresponding grade shall be used. When rainwater detention facilities need to be installed in the road median, the curb stone arrangement shall meet drainage requirements. 2.1.5 Bus-Only Lane 1. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 3 lanes or more (including 3 lanes), or the total one-way motor vehicle roadway width is not less than 11 m; where one-way passenger bus volume on the road section exceeds 6,000 persons/peak hour, or bus flow exceeds 150 vehicles/peak hour; and where the average section flow per lane exceeds 500 vehicles/peak hour. 2. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 4 lanes or more (including 4 lanes), and the one-way bus flow on the section exceeds 90 vehicles/peak hour. 3. Urban arterial roads shall be provided with bus-only lanes where the one-way motor vehicle lane count on a road section is 2 lanes, the one-way passenger bus volume exceeds 6,000 persons/peak hour, and bus flow exceeds 150 vehicles/peak hour. 29 4. Bus-only lanes may be paved with colored asphalt. After paving, the lane color is conspicuous and forms a sharp contrast with the adjacent ordinary motor vehicle lane, preventing ordinary motor vehicles from mistakenly entering the lane.
